blocks.text: DNA is present in the nucleus of every living cell. It is a coded plan, or blueprint, for making proteins, which are vital for life; each specific protein is made by a specific gene, a section of DNA. DNA carries the genetic instructions for the development, functioning, growth and reproduction of all living organisms. Its double helix stores information in the sequence of its four bases and passes it on efficiently and accurately for protein synthesis.

Genes are organised into larger units called chromosomes; humans receive 23 pairs from their parents. Nearly every cell carries the full set of 23 pairs, but each type of cell uses only some of its genes: a cell that will become a red blood cell switches on the gene for haemoglobin and keeps the gene for keratin switched off.

blocks.alt: Five linked circles, each a close-up of the one before: a cell with its nucleus (genome, in nucleus of cell); a chromosome (23 pairs in a human cell); a banded chromosome section with one gene marked (section of a chromosome that makes a single protein); a DNA double helix (polymer chains made up of bases attached to a sugar-phosphate chain); and three bases G, T, A on a backbone (codon, group of three bases which codes for a specific amino acid).

blocks.text: The structure and function of DNA

In 1953 James Watson and Francis Crick showed that DNA consists of two polynucleotide chains. Each chain forms a right-handed helix and the two chains coil round each other to form a double helix. The chains are not identical but complementary, and they run in opposite directions: the 3' end of one faces the 5' end of the other. Each chain has a sugar-phosphate backbone with bases projecting at right angles, held by weak hydrogen bonds to the bases of the other chain. Adenine (A) is always opposite thymine (T), and guanine (G) opposite cytosine (C); there are two hydrogen bonds in an A-T pair and three in a G-C pair.

blocks.alt: Left, base pairing: eight pairs between two vertical sugar-phosphate backbones, A-T, C-G, G-C, G-C, T-A, T-A, C-G, G-C; A-T pairs are joined by two dashed hydrogen bonds and G-C pairs by three. Right, double helix: two backbone ribbons winding round each other with coloured base pairs across.

blocks.text: Genes are the specific regions of DNA that carry genetic information and instruct the cell to make particular proteins. An important process of DNA is self-replication: during the cell cycle DNA is copied, so that at cell division each new cell receives a complete set of genetic material. In this way genetic information passes from one cell to its daughter cells and to the next generation.
